text: Sofia – The Bulgarian Communist Party has changed its name. It is now called the Bulgarian Socialist Party. Alexander Lilov remains as the party's chairman. Delegates at the party congress abandoned Marxism-Leninism and endorsed a multi-party system. The party has ruled the country for over forty years, and it adopts its new name ahead of the first free elections. Its main rival in those elections is the Union of Democratic Forces, which brings together more than ten opposition groups.

Sofia. The Great National Assembly has voted in favour of a new constitution for Bulgaria. It replaces the constitution that was in force under Tzvetan Zhivkov. The country is now becoming a parliamentary republic. The president will now be elected by the entire population, rather than by parliamentarians. The new constitution protects private property and freedom of belief. Parties formed on ethnic or religious grounds are prohibited. Some members of the opposition refused to sign the document. The Great National Assembly is now being dissolved, with new elections to take place in the country.

Sofia – Results have been announced from the elections to the Great National Assembly. The Bulgarian Socialist Party, formerly the communist party, secured 211 out of 400 seats. This marks the first multi-party elections in the country in over forty years. The Union of Democratic Forces came in second, winning in Sofia and other major cities. A second round was required in eighteen constituencies. The Great National Assembly will now be tasked with drafting a new constitution for the country. Students in Sofia are dissatisfied with the election results and have staged a sit-in strike at the university.

Sofia. Parliamentary elections have been held in Bulgaria under the new constitution. The Democratic Forces Union came first, securing 110 out of 240 seats. The Socialists, former communists, fell just four seats short. Third in the parliament were the Bulgarian Turks' party, the Movement for Rights and Freedoms, with 24 seats. For the first time since the war, Bulgaria's government will not be led by an ex-communist party. The lawyer Filip Dimitrov is likely to become prime minister.

Football news from Bulgaria. CSKA Sofia striker Hristo Stoichkov has been awarded the Golden Boot as Europe's top scorer. In the Bulgarian league, he scored thirty-eight goals in thirty matches. He shared the award with Real Madrid's Mexican player Hugo Sánchez, who also scored the same number of goals. Stoichkov is twenty-four years old and has been playing for CSKA for his fifth season. The club once again became Bulgarian champions this season. He is now moving to Barcelona, managed by Johan Cruyff.

Sofia. The Great National Assembly has elected Zelyu Zelyev as president of Bulgaria. He is fifty-five years old and is a philosopher, former dissident, and leader of the Union of Democratic Forces. In the 1960s, he was expelled from the party, and his book on fascism was withdrawn from stores just weeks after its publication. Zelyev is the first president of the country who was not a communist. His predecessor, Petar Mladenov, resigned following protests. General Atanas Semerdzhiev has been appointed vice-president.

Sofia. Todor Zhivkov is no longer in charge of Bulgaria. The plenum of the Central Committee accepted his resignation from the position of general secretary of the communist party, the day after the fall of the Berlin Wall. Zhivkov is seventy-eight years old. He had led the country for thirty-five years, longer than any other leader in Eastern Europe. The foreign minister, Petar Mladenov, has been chosen as the new general secretary. A week later, a large demonstration took place in the centre of Sofia, with people calling for free elections.

Czechoslovakia has held its first free elections in over forty years. Voter turnout was ninety-six per cent. The Civic Forum emerged as the winner in the Czech lands, while in Slovakia the movement “Public Against Violence” took first place. The Communist Party received around thirteen per cent of the votes and finished in second position. The new Federal Assembly will elect a president, with Václav Havel still being the leading candidate. New elections are scheduled to take place in two years, by which time deputies are expected to have drafted a constitution.

Prague. The Federal Assembly has unanimously elected Václav Havel as president of Czechoslovakia. He is a playwright whose plays were banned in his homeland for many years, and he was imprisoned earlier this spring. The day before, Alexander Dubček became president of the Federal Assembly, having led the country during the Prague Spring. The voting took place in the Old Town Hall in Prague. Immediately after his election, the new president went straight to attend a solemn mass at St. Vitus Cathedral.

Prague. The new Federal Assembly has once again elected Václav Havel as president of Czechoslovakia. Havel is fifty-three years old. Last time, he was elected by the deputies of the old parliament. This time, those elected in the first free elections cast their votes. His term as president this time is two years. During this period, the parliament must draft a new constitution, while the Czechs and Slovaks must decide how to move forward as one nation. Alexander Dubček has once again become the chairman of the Federal Assembly.

Prague. The country now has a new name: the Czech and Slovak Federal Republic. The word “socialist” was decided to be removed back in winter, and thereafter deputies debated for several weeks over how to spell the rest of the name. Slovak deputies wanted to use a hyphen to write “Czechoslovakia”, while the Czechs were opposed to this. In spring, two versions were even approved – one with a hyphen for Slovakia and one without for the Czech territories. Now the name includes both republics, and a hyphen is no longer needed. Newspapers have dubbed this dispute the “Hyphen War”.

The last Soviet troops have withdrawn from Czechoslovakia. They had been stationed there for over twenty years, since they suppressed the Prague Spring. The headquarters of the Central Group of Forces was located in Milovice, thirty-eight kilometres from Prague, where a tank division and air force were also based. Three more divisions were stationed in Mladá Boleslav, Vysoke Mýto and Bruntál, with one in the Slovakian town of Zvolen. In total, there were around eighty-five thousand Soviet soldiers in the country. The agreement regarding their withdrawal was signed in Moscow, and the troops left in successive convoys over the course of more than a year.

Prague. Police have dispersed a student demonstration on the National Avenue. Since then, protests have taken place every day, with hundreds of thousands gathering in Wenceslas Square. People are taking out keys and ringing them, as if sending the government home. The whole country held a two-hour general strike, during which factories, transport, and shops came to a standstill. The Communist Party has agreed to relinquish its leading role, while the Civil Forum, led by Václav Havel, is negotiating over a new government.

Football – the World Cup in Italy. The Czechoslovakian team has advanced to the quarter-finals. In their group stage, they beat the Americans 5–1 and the Austrians 1–0, losing only to Italy. In the round of 16, they crushed Costa Rica 4–1. Forward Tomáš Skuhravý scored all three goals, each time with his head, and now ranks among the tournament's top scorers. Their next opponent will be West Germany. The match takes place in Milan at the San Siro stadium, where the Germans have played throughout the tournament.

Moscow. Foreign ministers from both Germany, the Soviet Union, the United States, Great Britain, and France have signed the “Two Plus Four” agreement regarding the final settlement concerning Germany. The four powers are relinquishing all rights they acquired after the war, and a united Germany will become fully sovereign. Soviet troops will withdraw from its territory within the next four years. Germany's army will be reduced to three hundred seventy thousand men. The border with Poland along the Oder and Neisse rivers is being recognised as final.

Berlin. The checkpoint booth at Friedrichstrasse, known as “Checkpoint Charlie”, has been removed. For almost thirty years, foreigners, diplomats, and allied military personnel have used this crossing to travel between parts of Berlin. The booth was lifted away by crane. Ministers for foreign affairs from West and East Germany, the Soviet Union, the United States, Great Britain, and France attended the ceremony. On the same day, the ministers held another round of talks in Berlin regarding the future of Germany. The checkpoint itself remains in operation, and foreigners and diplomats continue to pass through as before.

East Germany has held its first parliamentary elections in free voting. Over ninety per cent of voters turned out to cast their ballots. The Alliance for Germany emerged as the winner, led by the East German Christian Democratic Union, which secured 192 out of 400 seats. The main promise of the victorious party is rapid reunification with West Germany. Lothar de Maizière, the leader of the Christian Democrats, will become prime minister, inviting social democrats to join his government.

East Germany has now adopted the West German mark. Salaries, pensions, scholarships, and rent have all been converted at a one-to-one rate. Savings are exchanged at varying rates depending on age: children under fourteen can exchange up to two thousand marks at a one-to-one rate, adults up to four thousand, and those over sixty up to six thousand. Anything exceeding these amounts is exchanged at a rate of two to one, and debts have also been halved. Ahead of the exchange, many people rushed to spend their old marks on washing machines and cars. Some handed over excess money to relatives so they could exchange it at a more favourable rate.

Good evening. This is your regular road-trip update. At midnight tonight, the German Democratic Republic ceased to exist, with its territories joining the Federal Republic. The black, red and gold flag has been raised in Berlin, and celebrations continued throughout the night in the streets. The country now has five new federal states: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia. East and West Berlin are now one city. This day has been declared a national holiday – Unity Day in Germany.

Berlin. The border between the two parts of the city has been opened. In the evening, at a press conference in East Berlin, Politburo member Günter Schabowski read out the new rules for travelling abroad. Journalists asked when the rules would come into effect, and he replied that they would apply immediately. A few hours later, thousands of people gathered at the checkpoint on Bornholmer Straße. The border guards had received no orders, so shortly before midnight they raised the barriers on their own. Other checkpoints were then opened as well, and that night, people from both sides of Berlin climbed onto the wall near the Brandenburg Gate.

Berlin. East German border guards have begun dismantling the Berlin Wall. Until now, it has been removed piece by piece by local residents and tourists using hammers and chisels. Now, cranes and heavy machinery are being employed. The concrete slabs are taken to landfills for disposal or recycling, while some are donated to museums and sold at auctions. The work is expected to take several years, as the wall stretched for over 150 kilometres. An opening was created at the Brandenburg Gate even before Christmas, and now people can walk along the former border zone.

Berlin. On an empty site between Potsdamer Platz and the Brandenburg Gate, where the former border strip once lay, Roger Waters performed Pink Floyd's “The Wall”. Joining him on stage were Scorpions, Cyndi Lauper, Sinéad O'Connor, Bryan Adams, Van Morrison, and Joni Mitchell. Throughout the evening, a wall made of polystyrene blocks was built on stage. A projection of a section of the real Berlin Wall was displayed on the blocks, and at the end, to the cheers of the audience, the wall was brought down. The concert was held to commemorate the fall of the wall, eight months after the borders were opened.

Hungary has opened its border with Austria to citizens of East Germany. Thousands of them have gathered there, having come for a holiday and unwilling to return home. The Hungarians began removing the barbed wire along this border as early as spring. At midnight, the barriers were raised, and queues of Trabants and Wartburgs headed west. Thousands of people crossed the border in the first few days. From Austria, the journey continues on to West Germany, where they are immediately given their own passports.

Budapest. Hungary has elected a new parliament following a two-round vote that marked the first free elections in over forty years. The Hungarian Democratic Forum emerged as the winner, with its leader Józef Antall set to become prime minister. He will form a coalition government with the Party of Small Landowners and the Christian Democrats. The Free Democrats finished in second place. The former ruling Socialist Party secured only thirty-three seats, finishing in fourth place. The Young Democrats from Fides also made it into parliament.

Budapest. Arpad Günth has been elected president of Hungary. He is sixty-eight years old and is a writer and translator. He was sentenced to life imprisonment for his involvement in an uprising against Soviet rule, but was released several years later as part of an amnesty. Since then, he has translated works by English and American authors into Hungarian, including Tolkien's “The Lord of the Rings”. Hungarians were able to decide via referendum whether to elect a president by popular vote, but too few people turned out to vote, so Günth was chosen by the parliament. He is the first head of state in Hungary in forty-two years who is not a communist.

Road Racing – Hungarian Grand Prix. At the Hungaroring, Belgian driver Thierry Boutsen won aboard a Williams. He started from pole position and led the entire race. His teammate Riccardo Patrese finished just four hundredths of a second behind him. Ayrton Senna in a McLaren was less than three tenths of a second behind, although he was involved in a collision with Alessandro Nannini during the race. Alain Prost retired from the competition, allowing Senna to widen his lead in the championship. It was Boutsen's first pole position of his career and his third Formula One victory.

Budapest. Tributes were paid today in Heroes' Square to Imre Nagy, the prime minister during the uprising against Soviet rule more than thirty years ago. Following the uprising, he was tried and executed, and his body was buried in an unmarked grave. Now, Nagy and his fellow rebels have been rehabilitated and reburied with full honours. People lined the streets beside coffins adorned with flowers, and the ceremony was broadcast on television. Members of the current government were among those standing at attention in honour of the deceased. Just a year ago, the authorities had even prohibited access to the site where he was buried.

Shopron. At the border with Austria, the Pan-European Picnic event took place today. Organisers agreed to open the old wooden gates on the road to Bratislava for a few hours. Among the guests were hundreds of citizens from East Germany who had come to Hungary for a holiday. They rushed towards the gates and crossed into Austria, with Hungarian border guards failing to stop them. In total, 661 people crossed to the other side that day. From Austria, the East Germans continued on their journey to West Germany.

Budapest. Hungary is no longer a people's republic. From the balcony of parliament, acting president Matyas Szurös declared the establishment of the Hungarian Republic. This took place on the anniversary of the uprising against Soviet rule. Tens of thousands of people gathered in the square in front of parliament. A week earlier, MPs had approved nearly a hundred amendments to the constitution. From now on, the country will have multiple political parties, free elections, and a separation of powers. The ruling party has also changed its name, now calling itself the Hungarian Socialist Party.

Budapest. The last Soviet troops have left Hungary. The Southern Group of Forces had been stationed in the country for over thirty years, and it has now been disbanded. The agreement regarding their withdrawal was signed in Moscow, and the withdrawal process took more than a year, with units departing eastward in successive trains. The final fighter-bombers took off from Kunmádárás airfield in the spring, being transferred to Volgograd. An infantry division had moved to the Kyiv Military District as early as winter. The last trains departed via the Záhony border station. The barracks and airfields are now empty.
The news.

Football, the World Cup in Italy. In the opening match, Cameroon defeated the reigning champions Argentina 1–0 at a stadium in Milan. The goal was scored by François Omam-Biyik with a head strike. Cameroon later reached the quarter-finals, a feat no African team had achieved before. The top scorer for Cameroon was Roger Milla, with four goals. He is 38 years old, has already retired from international football, but returned at the request of his country's president. After each of Milla's goals, he dances by the corner flag.

Football: the World Cup final was held at the Olympic Stadium in Rome. West Germany defeated Argentina 1–0. The only goal was scored by Andreas Brehme from a penalty with five minutes left in the match. The penalty was awarded by Mexican referee Edgardo Codesal, and two Argentine players were shown red cards. Germany became world champions for the third time. Franz Beckenbauer had won the tournament as a player, and now he had also won it as a coach. Four years earlier, the same teams met in the final, with Argentina coming out on top at that time.

Athletics – World Championships in Tokyo. Twenty-seven-year-old American Mike Powell jumped for 8.95 metres in the long jump. This sets a new world record, achieved at the Tokyo National Stadium. The previous record, held by Bob Beamon at 8.90 metres, had stood for almost twenty-three years. Carl Lewis, who set a world record in the 100 metres just five days earlier, jumped 8.91 metres in the same event, but under headwind, finishing in second place. Lewis had not lost a long jump competition in ten years.

Tennis – the U.S. Open in New York. Nineteen-year-old American Pete Sampras has won his first Grand Slam tournament. He defeated Andre Agassi in the final: 6–4, 6–3, 6–2. Agassi is twenty years old and had already lost the final at Roland Garros this season. Sampras was born in Washington. His parents are from Greece. He has become the youngest champion in the history of this tournament. On his way to the title, he also beat Ivan Lendl and John McEnroe, despite being seeded only twelfth in the competition.

Football, the World Cup semi-final in Turin. West Germany defeated England on penalties. The regular time and extra time ended in a 1-1 draw. The Germans took the lead with a shot from Bremé, the ball bouncing over the goalkeeper. Gary Lineker equalised with ten minutes left. The English midfielder Paul Gascoigne was shown a yellow card, which would mean he missed the final, and he cried on the pitch. In the penalty shoot-out, the English players Stuart Pearce and Chris Waddle missed their shots. In the final, Germany will play Argentina.

Tennis, Wimbledon. The final saw two Germans meet, with the underdog emerging victorious. Twenty-two-year-old Michael Stich beat Boris Becker in three sets: 6–4, 7–6, 6–4. Becker is twenty-three, having won his first Wimbledon title at the age of seventeen. He has won this tournament three times and entered the final as the clear favourite. Stich, meanwhile, had defeated last year's champion Stefan Edberg in the semi-finals, not breaking Edberg's serve once throughout the match. It was the first time in Wimbledon's history that a final has been contested by two Germans.

Sports – Tour de France. Spanish rider Miguel Indurain of the Banesto team has claimed victory in the world's premier multi-day race. He is originally from Navarre, and his team also won the team classification. As usual, the finish line was located on the Champs-Élysées in Paris. The favorite to win was American Greg LeMond, who had won two previous Tours in a row, but he fell behind during the mountain stages in the Pyrenees. Indurain is twenty-seven years old. He was previously known as a helper to the leaders, but now he is the leading figure in Spanish cycling.

Tokyo. Mike Tyson has lost for the first time in his career. He had previously won all thirty-seven of his fights, with his last opponent managing to last only ninety-three seconds against him. The bout for the world heavyweight championship took place at the Tokyo Dome. Tyson was the clear favourite, with odds in his favour at forty-two to one against his opponent, James Douglas. In the eighth round, Douglas was knocked down, and in the tenth round, he himself knocked Tyson out. The new world champion is Buster Douglas.

Edirne. Turks continue to arrive from Bulgaria via the Kapıkule border crossing. The Bulgarian authorities describe this as a tourist trip, but the people are crossing with their belongings and families, many of them for good. More than three hundred thousand people have crossed the border since the start of summer. Turkey allowed everyone in, even without visas, and refugees have been housed in tent camps or with relatives. Now Ankara is reintroducing visas for holders of Bulgarian passports, effectively closing the border. Many of those who have left are already returning.

Good evening. This is your regular road-trip update. We're hearing that Turkey has now begun filling the reservoir behind the Atatürk Dam on the Euphrates River. Construction on the dam has been underway for seven years now. The river has been almost completely blocked off for the past month. Syria and Iraq were warned in advance, back in the autumn, but both countries have expressed their objection. The dam is 169 metres high, and the reservoir will cover an area of over 800 square kilometres. It will be the third-largest reservoir in Turkey, after Lake Van and Lake Tuz. The power station and irrigation channels are set to provide electricity and water to the southeast of the country. That's all for now. Stay safe on the road.

Brussels. The European Commission has responded to Turkey's application to join the European Community. Ankara submitted the request almost three years ago. The Community currently comprises twelve countries, the latest to join being Spain and Portugal. The Commission confirmed that Turkey could become a member, but it is too early to begin negotiations. Reasons cited include the country's economy, its domestic policy, relations with Greece, and the dispute over Cyprus. The Turkish government is disappointed, but it is not withdrawing its application.

Ankara. Early parliamentary elections have taken place in Turkey. The True Path Party led by Süleyman Demirel came first, followed by the ruling Fatherland Party in second place, with the Social Democrats finishing in third. Demirel, who has been removed from power twice by the military, will once again become prime minister. He will now need to form a coalition, with the Social Democratic People's Party led by Erdal İnönü being the most likely partner. President Turgut Özal remains in his position, while his former party moves into opposition.

Ankara. The Grand National Assembly has elected Turgut Özal as President of Turkey. He is sixty-two years old and is an electrical engineer by training. He served as Prime Minister for the past six years and led the Fatherland Party. Özal is the first civilian president to hold the position in thirty years. Prior to him, the role was occupied by military figures. Yıldırım Akbulut has been appointed as the new Prime Minister. The opposition did not participate in the voting. The new president will move into the Çankaya residence on the hill above Ankara.

Istanbul. Turkey's first private television channel, Star, has now begun broadcasting. Until now, television in Turkey has been entirely state-run, and legislation currently prohibits private channels. As a result, Star transmits from abroad, with its signal sent via satellite from West Germany and using studios belonging to Germany's Sat 1. The channel airs programmes in the evenings, from six to eleven. It was founded by Cem Uzan and Ahmet Özal, the president's son. The programme schedule features foreign series and music videos.

A special day for fans at the Tracen Academy! The doors will be open all day, with each class having its own booth. Swip Tosho, Biko Pegasus, Mayano Top Gun, and Nisino Flower will perform together in a magical show. Matikanefukukitaru and Meisho Dotto will read fortunes for anyone who wishes. In the evening, there will be a concert featuring the season's winners on stage!

Horse racing news! The Kikuka Sho race over three thousand metres was held in Kyoto, and Matikanefukukitaru emerged as the winner. She stayed in the middle of the pack for most of the distance, before overtaking all competitors from the outside on the final straight. As usual, Fukukitaru prayed to the great Shiraoki before the race. After crossing the finish line, she said that an early morning divination had promised her great luck.

News from Hanshin. The Kobe Shimbun-hai has won the Matikané Fukukitaru race! Silence Suzuki led for most of the distance, but Fukukitaru accelerated in the final straight and overtook her. Suzuki congratulated her rival, though she remained puzzled as to what fortune-telling had to do with it. This is Fukukitaru's second consecutive victory, and she is now heading to the Kikuka-shō race. She has promised not to change her talismans until autumn.

News from Ritto's dormitory! Roommates Matikanefukukitaru and Matikane Tannhoyzer have once again been making noise right up until curfew. Their room in the dormitory has even earned the nickname “the room of sudden screams”. Air Shakur, who lives next door, has asked us to pass on a message saying everyone is tired and wants to sleep. Here it is! Girls, please speak more quietly, at least after ten o'clock.

Good afternoon, racing listeners! At the academy, Matikané Fukukitaru and Meishō Doto's fortune-telling booth is once again open for business. The queue has been forming since early morning, with people seeking predictions on everything from the weather and exams to horse racing results. Doto admits that she herself believes in every forecast given. If you're facing bad luck, don't worry – protective charms are available at the table next to them. Fukukitaru personally selected these charms.

Kinen Takaradzuka has won the Gold Spike for the second consecutive year! It was held at Hanshin Racecourse, over 2,200 metres in length. As usual, she started when she chose to, and then pulled away from all the others by staying on the outside lane. No one knows what Gold Spike will do after crossing the finish line, not even her trainer. This time, she performed her own unique routine on stage, and the audience loved it!

Good afternoon from Tennō-shō at 3,200 metres, and once again, Meziro Makkuin claims victory in Kyoto! This is her second consecutive win in this race. The renowned Makkuin family is very proud of their successor. Meziro herself has asked that no questions be asked about sweets, as she is on a strict diet. However, following such a remarkable victory, her trainer has allowed her to have one small piece of cake.

Arima Kinen at Nakayama! Oguri Cap has won her farewell race. Many thought her best days were behind her, but she came in first, with the stands chanting her name. The “grey monster,” as her fans call her, is said to have eaten three servings of rice after the race. The chefs at the Tracen Academy are already preparing for a celebration.

From Kyoto's Kikuka-cho, an unexpected winner has emerged! Rhys Shawer outpaced Mihono Bourbon, who was aiming for a triple crown. Earlier in the season, Bourbon had won the Satsuki-cho race as well as the Japanese Derby, staying unbeaten throughout. The stands fell silent – no one had anticipated such an outcome. Rhys Shawer is a quiet and modest horse, yet she never faltered on the track. Congratulations!

A big day in Tokyo! Speshal Week has won the Tokyo Yushun, Japan's most famous horse race! She came to the track from Hokkaido, having promised her mother she would become Japan's best runner. The stands erupted as she took the lead in the final two hundred metres. Right after crossing the finish line, Speshal Week asked when dinner would be. Her trainer says this is a good sign.

Japan Cup in Tokyo! Two thousand four hundred metres – the best female runners from Japan and guests from Europe taking off, and it's Special Week who wins! The Frenchwoman was considered the favourite. They were neck and neck in the final metres, yet it was Special Week who crossed the finish line first. Everyone at Trassen was glued to the TVs in the dormitory. Silence Suzuki was the first to send her congratulations.

Takaradzuka Kinen's Hanshin has taken the lead from the very first metre and has held off all challengers. She finished with a substantial margin ahead of the rest. Suzuki admits that what she enjoys most is having the track clear in front of her. Her companion, Fukukitaru Matikané, predicted the outcome of this race and has promised to forecast the next one as well.

Summer training by the sea! Swip Tosho has taught Fusaiti Pandora a spell to combat the heat. The spell turns out to be a hose with cold water. Pandora isn't upset at all and now calls her “grandma,” as Swipi had previously taught Rain Craft magic as well. And Fujikiiseki is once again trying to persuade her to finish eating her vegetables. So far, without success, especially with the peppers.

Another victory for Swift Tojo! In Kyoto, she won the Queen Elizabeth Cup. She already claimed the Takaradzuka Kinen this season, and now she has added this cup to her collection. After the race, she called the studio and asked that she not be referred to as Swift Tojo on air – it is merely a pseudonym. We'll correct that. It was the magical Swiftie who won! Reports suggest she will celebrate with the largest parfait in the café.

News from Kyoto. Shuka-sho has won the Swip Tosho race! It is her first victory in a major race. This morning, she declared that she did not wish to compete, and she was persuaded until just before the start. But during the race, Swip Tosho caught up with all the other horses on the final straight. She had given her hat, a gift from her grandmother, to someone to hold before the start, and ran after it right after crossing the finish line.

A sensational finish at Hanshin! Kinen Takaradzuka has won the Swip Tosho race! Two thousand two hundred metres of track, with the stands completely full. On the final straight, she overtook everyone, leaving Zennno Rob Roy behind. Rob Roy has already promised to fight back this autumn – after all, they are both friends and rivals. Kinen Takaradzuka herself described it as a spell, though she refused to reveal which one – it's a secret kept by the magician.

Arima Kinen at Nakayama! Tokai Teio has returned after a full year away from racing and has won! Exactly one year ago, she ran here too but finished well behind. She was under treatment, trained hard again, and many had given up on seeing her compete. At the finish line, she was crying, and half of the stands were crying with her. Teio's famous stride is back on the track!

Haru Urara has finished last once again! And once more, the stands gave her the loudest applause of all, with fans carrying her tickets as talismans. She competes at the small Koti racetrack, running in every race as if it were the final, never losing heart. Haru Urara says she's determined to overtake at least one of her rivals next time. We here in the studio are cheering for her!

The Channel Tunnel. Workers constructing the tunnel beneath the strait met at its midpoint. Construction had been carried out from both sides – from the English port of Folkestone and from the French port of Coquelles. Englishman Graham Fagg and Frenchman Philippe Cozzet broke through the final barrier in the service tunnel and shook hands in front of the cameras. For the first time since the Ice Age, Britain and the European mainland are connected by land. The tunnel is approximately fifty kilometres long. It is expected to open in a few years, with trains and cars set to travel through it.

Space news. The Space Shuttle Discovery has successfully placed the Hubble telescope into orbit. Named after astronomer Edwin Hubble, the telescope features a mirror with a diameter of just over two and a half metres. It took more than ten years to develop, but the initial images turned out to be blurry. Engineers discovered that the main mirror had been polished incorrectly – a mistake smaller than the thickness of a hair, yet sufficient to blur the images. The telescope will need to be repaired in orbit, requiring a separate mission by astronauts.

Good evening. This is your regular road-trip update. Overnight, Iraq has moved troops into neighbouring Kuwait. Within just a few hours, the Iraqi army seized the capital, forcing Kuwait's emir to flee to Saudi Arabia. The United Nations Security Council has called for the withdrawal of Iraqi forces and imposed trade sanctions against Iraq in response. In retaliation, Iraq has declared Kuwait to be one of its provinces. The United States is sending troops to Saudi Arabia. Oil prices are rising rapidly – from seventeen dollars per barrel before the invasion, they are now above thirty dollars. Petrol prices have also increased at filling stations across Europe.

Cape Town. Nelson Mandela has been released. He was set free by President Frederik de Klerk, who had earlier lifted the ban on the African National Congress. Mandela spent twenty-seven years in prison, first on Robben Island and then in the prisons of Pollsmoor and Victor Verster. He stepped out of the prison gates holding his wife Winnie's hand. Crowds gathered to welcome him, and television stations broadcast the moment live to audiences around the world. In the evening, Mandela addressed the city's residents from the balcony of Cape Town's town hall.

Moscow. The first McDonald's in the Soviet Union has opened on Pushkin Square. Queues formed early in the morning, and the restaurant served around thirty-eight thousand customers in its first day – a record for the company. With seven hundred seats, it is the largest McDonald's in the world. The opening was facilitated by the company's Canadian branch, led by George Cohen. Negotiations to establish the restaurant took fourteen years. Payments can only be made in rubles, with a Big Mac costing three rubles and seventy-five kopecks.

Oslo. The President of the Soviet Union, Mikhail Gorbachev, has been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. The Nobel Committee highlighted his role in bringing an end to the Cold War. Gorbachev is the first Soviet leader to receive this honour. In recent years, Germany has been reunified, and the countries of Eastern Europe have been able to choose their own path, with Moscow not interfering. Gorbachev himself will not be attending the ceremony in Oslo. One of his deputy foreign ministers will receive the prize on his behalf. The laureate will deliver his Nobel lecture at a later date.

Alps. On a glacier near the Tisenjoch pass, on the border between Austria and Italy, German tourists Helmut and Erika Zimon discovered a human body frozen inside the ice. The body was located at an altitude of over three thousand metres. At first, they thought it might be that of a deceased mountaineer. However, the person was wearing leather clothing and a cloak made of grass, and nearby lay a copper axe, a bow, and a quiver of arrows. An archaeologist from Innsbruck believes the find is at least four thousand years old. Scientists in Innsbruck have already begun referring to it as the Ice Man.

Space news. The American Voyager 1 probe has taken a final image of the solar system. Its camera was turned toward Earth, and from a distance of over six billion kilometres, the probe captured a photograph of our planet. This is the farthest image of Earth ever taken. In the picture, Earth appears smaller than a single dot, hanging in a beam of sunlight like a speck of dust. The idea to take this image came from astronomer Carl Sagan. Voyager has been in flight for thirteen years now, and its cameras will now be switched off to conserve energy.

Moscow. Mikhail Gorbachev has stepped down as President of the Soviet Union. He had led the country for almost seven years, and his address to the citizens was broadcast on television. The presidential powers, including control over nuclear weapons, have been transferred to Russia's President Boris Yeltsin. In the evening, the red flag of the Soviet Union was lowered from the Kremlin, and the Russian tricolour was raised in its place. Shortly before this, leaders of Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus had agreed in the Belovezh Forest to form the Commonwealth of Independent States. The Soviet Union no longer exists.

Geneva. At the European Organization for Nuclear Research, CERN, British programmer Tim Berners-Lee devised the World Wide Web. He first outlined the project two years earlier. It is a method of linking documents on different computers through hyperlinks. By clicking on a word, you can be taken to a page located on the other side of the world. The first server for the Web operates at CERN on a computer belonging to the company NexT. Initially, only physicists used the Web, but now the software is available to anyone connected to the Internet.

Moscow. For the first time in Russia, a president has been elected by the entire population. Boris Yeltsin, chairman of the Russian Supreme Soviet, was the winner, having received votes from over half of the electorate, so a second round will not take place. Yeltsin is sixty years old and left the Communist Party a year ago. Alexander Ruzskoy will become vice-president. Former Soviet Union prime minister Nikolai Ryzhkov received less than twenty per cent of the votes. On the same day, residents of Leningrad voted to restore the city's name to St Petersburg.

Basketball – The Yugoslavian national team has won the world championship. The final tournament was held in Buenos Aires at the Luna Park arena, where the Yugoslavs defeated the Soviet Union side in the final. Tony Kukoč was named the tournament's most valuable player. Centre Vlade Divac, who plays for the Los Angeles Lakers in the National Basketball Association, was also included in the all-star team. Just a year earlier, the same team won the European championship in Zagreb. The team is coached by Dušan Ivković.

Belgrade. Yugoslavia has carried out a currency reform. The new dinar is equal to ten thousand of the old ones, with four zeros removed from the banknotes. Prime Minister Ante Marković aims to curb inflation, as prices have risen by more than ten times over the past year. The new dinar is pegged to the West German mark at seven dinars to the mark, and it can be freely exchanged at banks. Salaries have been frozen for six months. Old banknotes are still accepted in shops alongside the new ones. The largest old note, worth two million dinars, is now worth two hundred new dinars.

In Slovenia and Croatia, multi-party elections have taken place for the first time in forty-five years. In Slovenia, the opposition coalition Demos secured more than half of the votes, while Milan Kucan, former leader of the Slovenian communists, was elected chairman of the republic's presidium. In Croatia, the Croatian Democratic Union came out on top, winning 205 out of 356 seats. Its leader, Franjo Tuđman, will become chairman of the republic's presidium. The Croatian Communist Party has moved to the opposition for the first time since the war.

Belgrade. The emergency congress of the Union of Communists of Yugoslavia has been suspended. Delegates gathered to decide how to move forward for the party that has ruled the country since the war began. For two days, delegates from Serbia and Slovenia debated how much power the republics should retain. The majority rejected all of the Slovenian proposals, and the Slovenian delegation left the Sava Centre hall. The Croatian delegation stated that it would not continue without the Slovenians. Around eleven o'clock at night, the congress chairman, Milan Pancevski, adjourned the meeting until the morning, but the congress was not reconvened in the morning.

Football: Champions League final in Bari. Red Star from Belgrade defeated the French team Marseille. Regular time and extra time ended goalless, with the match decided by a penalty shootout, 5 to 3. The Belgrade side converted all five of their penalties, with Darko Pančev scoring the final one. It was the first Champions League title in Yugoslavian football history. Before the final, the team was based in Monopoli, forty kilometres from Bari, and thousands of fans travelled from Yugoslavia to watch the match.

Ljubljana. Slovenia has voted in a referendum in favour of independence. Over ninety per cent of voters turned out to cast their ballots, with nearly ninety-six per cent voting in favour. This represents eighty-eight and a half per cent of the country's total electorate, exceeding the threshold required by law. If no agreement can be reached regarding the new structure for Yugoslavia within six months, the republic will declare itself an independent state. The results were announced in the parliament by its president, Franče Bučar.

Football – the quarter-finals of the World Cup in Florence, at the Artemio Franchi stadium. Yugoslavia were defeated by reigning world champions Argentina on penalties. The Yugoslavs played almost the entire match with ten men after a red card in the first half. No goals were scored in regular time or extra time. Even Maradona missed in the penalty shoot-out, but Argentina's goalkeeper Sergio Goycochea saved two attempts, allowing Argentina to win 3–2. In the semi-finals, they will face the host nation, Italy.
